Part 2 — Test-Style Questions (12 questions · hard and very hard)

Twelve questions, hardest last. Write your answer in the box — there are no options to choose from, so show the working that gets you there. Run the two-question test on every one: was selection random? (how far it generalises) and was assignment random? (whether cause may be claimed). They are independent.

#LevelQuestionAnswerSolution
P1Hard
Researchers recorded the diets and blood pressure of 500 adults who had each chosen their own diet, and found that a high-salt diet was associated with higher blood pressure. State the best-supported conclusion.
There is an association between the two, but the study cannot establish cause.

Nobody was assigned a diet, so this is an observational study and only association follows.

Two common wrong answers assert a direction of cause the design cannot support.

P2Hard
In a study, 300 volunteers are randomly assigned to either a new tutoring method or the usual one, and the new method's group scores higher. State the best-supported conclusion.
The new method causes higher scores for people like these volunteers.

Random assignment supports a causal claim, but the volunteers were not randomly selected, so the finding cannot be stretched beyond people like them.

A common wrong answer is the classic overreach.

P3Hard
A study finds that towns with more public parks have lower obesity rates. Which is the most plausible confounding variable?
The average household income of the town.

A confounder must plausibly affect both quantities. Wealthier towns tend to have more parks and lower obesity.

Two common wrong answers name the two variables already in the study.

P4Hard
A researcher randomly selects 200 students from one school and surveys them about study habits. To which group may the results be generalised?
All students at that school.

The sample was drawn at random from that school, so the conclusion extends to that school and no further.

A common wrong answer is too cautious: random sampling is exactly what licenses the step from sample to school.

P5Hard
A survey of 400 people reports a margin of error of 5 percentage points. The researchers repeat it with 1,600 people, sampled the same biased way. Which improves?
Precision only; the estimate is still centred on the wrong value.

A larger sample narrows the margin of error, so the estimate becomes more precise.

But the same flawed selection means it is still precisely wrong. Size does not fix bias.

P6Very
hard
Two studies are described. Study 1 randomly selects 500 adults from a city and surveys their exercise habits. Study 2 takes 500 volunteers and randomly assigns them to two exercise programmes. State the best-supported conclusion.
Study 1 supports generalisation to the city; Study 2 supports a causal claim for its participants.

Random selection (Study 1) buys generalisation; random assignment (Study 2) buys cause.

A common wrong answer swaps them, which is the error the question is built around.

P7Very
hard
A newspaper reports: ‘Students who eat breakfast score higher on tests, so schools should provide breakfast.’ The data came from a survey of students' existing habits. What is the main flaw?
The recommendation assumes cause from an observational study.

The survey recorded what students already did, so it shows association only. Families who provide breakfast may differ in other ways.

The recommendation needs an experiment behind it.

P8Very
hard
A clinical trial randomly assigns 300 patients, all recruited from one hospital, to a drug or a placebo. The drug group improves significantly more. State the best-supported conclusion.
The drug caused the improvement in this group of patients.

Random assignment establishes cause within the trial.

Recruitment from a single hospital is not random selection from any wider population, so A over-reaches; C under-reads the assignment.

P9Very
hard
A researcher wants to estimate the average commute time of all adults in a city and surveys every adult leaving one train station at 8 a.m. Which single change would most improve the study?
Select adults at random from the city's electoral register.

The flaw is the sampling frame: train users are not all adults, and no sample size fixes that.

Only random selection from the whole population does. A common wrong answer makes a biased estimate more precise, not more accurate.

P10Very
hard
In an experiment, 250 adults on diet A improved by a mean of 6.4 units and 250 on diet B by a mean of 4.1 units. Assignment was random. What is the difference in mean improvement?
2.3

6.4 − 4.1 = 2.3 units.

Because assignment was random, this difference can reasonably be attributed to the diets.

P11Very
hard
A town has 24,000 adults. A random sample estimates 38% support for a proposal, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Approximately how many adults does the lower end of the plausible interval represent?
8400

Lower end = 38 − 3 = 35%.

0.35 × 24,000 = 8,400 adults.

P12Very
hard
Of 500 adults in an observational study, 180 reported a high-salt diet. What percentage of the sample is this?
36

180/500 = 0.36 = 36%.

Note this is a statistic about the sample; extending it to the population needs the sample to have been randomly selected.

The one habit to build. Selection and assignment are two different things and answer two different questions. Most wrong answers on this topic are true statements about the wrong group, or causal claims from data where nobody assigned anything.
